extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and peer reviewers (scientific community)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or implementing the publication of anonymized referee reports, editorial decision letters, and author rebuttals as part of a journal's supplementary information to increase transparency in peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency as a fundamental guiding principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency in science: each experiment, each theoretical derivation needs to be documented and verifiable. Transparency promotes and drives scientific progress and ensures that scientific results are accountable to the highest standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a normative basis for arguing that peer review discussions, like experiments and derivations, are valuable when documented and accessible. The editorial frames transparency as generally beneficial unless constrained by confidentiality (e.g., corporate research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of anonymous referee reports and editorial decision letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Would the publication of anonymous referee reports and editorial decision letters of published papers benefit the scientific debate? The EMBO Journal trial published a Peer Review File containing decision letters, anonymized referee reports, and author rebuttal letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EMBO trial is presented as a concrete model: include decision letters (which contain anonymized reports) and rebuttal letters as supplementary material for papers that opt in.

rubrics_metrics.name: EMBO Peer Review File contents (decision letters, anonymized reports, rebuttals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Peer Review File provides, amongst other data, the decision letters from editors to authors, which include the anonymized referee reports, as well as the rebuttal letters from the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies what documents were published in the trial—use this set as a template for what to disclose when publishing peer review materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal influence on the conventional peer review process
rubrics_metrics.description: A model that minimally influences the conventional process is more likely to succeed while delivering transparency benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EMBO approach is highlighted as successful because it does not alter the normal review workflow substantially; this is presented as an advantage over models that change process (e.g., open public peer review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Author consent and reviewer willingness
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical viability depends on participants: almost 95% of authors agreed to take part in EMBO's trial, and only a few reviewers declined to review under the condition of having their reports published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and account for opt-in/opt-out rates among authors and reviewers as part of assessing feasibility and acceptability of publishing peer review materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community interest measured by download rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Download rates of published peer review files are an indicator of community interest; in the trial, download rates were about 10% of that of the corresponding papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use download metrics to judge uptake and utility; note the observed pattern that the files of papers considered the 'best' by editors, rather than controversial papers, attracted most downloads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility and accountability of editorial contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing review files makes the editor's contributions more visible and subjects editorial decisions to increased scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increased visibility is framed positively—editors 'have to take responsibility for the decisions that we take'—and is given as a justification for publishing review correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceability of paper improvements during peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which a paper has been improved during the peer review process becomes more obvious when review correspondence is published; reviewer input becomes more identifiable and recognizable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use published review files to show substantive changes and improvements between initial submission and final paper; this documents the value added by peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential influence on reviewer behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers will be aware that their comments could get published, which may influence their relationship with editors and the tone or content of reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider possible behavioral changes (positive or chilling) among reviewers when deciding whether and how to publish reports; monitor for changes in report style or candor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: informal communications not captured
rubrics_metrics.description: There might still be parts of the editorial process that would not necessarily be apparent; informal communication between authors and editors as well as reviewers takes place and may not be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that publishing official correspondence does not capture all interactions; ensure stakeholders understand this limitation when interpreting published files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review pitfalls (low uptake, low-quality comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review—public peer review with comment posting—had low uptake and generally low technical quality in Nature's trial, leading to abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an anti-pattern: fully open public commenting on submissions may not produce high-quality technical feedback or sufficient engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-blind peer review pitfalls (difficulty concealing identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-blind peer review, where author identity is withheld, can be difficult in practice to achieve because colleagues can often infer authorship (e.g., APS experiments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims of fully concealment with caution; empirical results suggest blinding can be imperfect and should be considered when designing review models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review discussions are valuable beyond publication decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The issues raised during the peer review process constitute an important contribution to the scientific debate and have value beyond their immediate purpose of deciding whether to publish a paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use publication of review correspondence to make these debates accessible to the broader community, thereby enriching post-publication discussion and verification.
